title: I inherited three paid-off properties at 23. How do I build on them?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #246 | INHERITANCE PASSED DOWN BY MOM
excerpt: A 23-year-old nurse in Singapore inherited three fully paid properties and wants ten rentals one day. Sean says settle the brother's care first, then learn before borrowing against anything.

qa.asker: MK, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: MK, 23, is a Malaysian with Singapore PR working as a nurse in Singapore, earning about RM100,000 a year. MK's mother recently passed away, leaving three fully paid properties: a two-storey terrace house rented out for RM3,600, a two-storey office lot previously rented for RM5,000, and a single-storey terrace house in Batu Pahat, plus RM150,000 in cash. MK also looks after an elder brother with special needs, whose care costs about RM2,000 a month.
qa.question: How can MK use refinancing, collateral and the rental income to build a lifetime portfolio of ten rental properties?
qa.quote: Start building from now, assuming you have nothing.
qa.answer: Not yet. First decide how the brother will be cared for, because that decides where MK works and so what income the banks will see. Then treat the inheritance as untouchable for the next five to eight years, keep the cash safe, and spend that time learning how property investing works before borrowing against anything.

reasons.title: Refinancing still needs an income
reasons.body: Paid-off properties can't simply be pushed to a bank for cash: the bank must see enough income to service the new loan. Staying in Singapore or coming home to give care changes that income completely.

reasons.title: The rent already covers the care
reasons.body: About RM8,600 a month in rent from fully paid properties can pay for professional care, even at RM5,000 to RM6,000 a month, while MK keeps the Singapore career. The mother has already done the heavy lifting.

reasons.title: A young heir attracts sales pitches
reasons.body: People close to MK know about the inheritance and may push mutual funds, policies or ventures. Whether these are right depends on knowledge MK doesn't have yet, so stay discreet and sign nothing in a hurry.

reasons.title: The income is already ahead
reasons.body: At 23, MK earns what many in Kuala Lumpur only reach as managers in their late twenties, and Malaysian banks assess Singapore income like a local's. That is a strong base to build on with MK's own credit.

actions: Decide on your brother's care first: yourself, a home helper or a professional facility.
Keep the RM150,000 in fixed deposit until you know what you want to do with it.
Work through Sean's four basic steps: set your intent, find your loan eligibility, view properties, then decide.
Learn how to manage tenants, declare rental income so it counts for future loans, and check that rent covers the instalment.
When you do borrow, take enough mortgage insurance (MRTA or MLTA) so your loans never pass to your family as debts.
qa.caveat: MK's plans may change within a few years, such as settling in Singapore, where buying an HDB flat would affect how they invest in Malaysia. Sean leaves what and where to buy until MK understands the rules.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #246. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in April 2024. Sean recommends FAR Capital, a property investment club he says he is a member of, not an owner, and earns from what it sells; the article leaves out that recommendation.
